chapters.title: The Early Republic and the Struggle of the Orders
chapters.body:
Every account of early Rome begins with a confession. The narrative historians on whom we depend, Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, wrote under Augustus, more than four centuries after the events they describe. The first Roman to write history, Quintus Fabius Pictor, worked around 200 BC, and he wrote in Greek. What lay behind them was thin: the list of annual magistrates (the fasti), the annual record kept by the pontifex maximus (the annales maximi, later worked up into eighty books), the texts of a few treaties and laws, temple foundation dates, and the self-serving traditions of great families. Livy himself admits (6.1) that most records perished when the Gauls burned the city. The modern historian therefore works with two kinds of evidence that rarely meet: a literary tradition full of moralising set-pieces, and an archaeological record that is mute about politics. The usual compromise, argued most influentially by T. J. Cornell, is to trust the 'structural facts' (institutions, laws, treaties, the outline of the fasti) while treating the stories that clothe them as later dramatisation. Dates in this chapter are Varronian, the system fixed in the late Republic; for the fourth century they run about three years ahead of the Greek synchronisms, which is why the anarchy and the 'dictator years' were invented to stretch the calendar.

The end of the monarchy, conventionally 509 BC, was probably not a popular revolution but an aristocratic coup against an overmighty king, Tarquinius Superbus ([[tarquinius_superbus|Tarquinius Superbus]]). The story of Lucretia's rape and suicide and the oath of [[lucius_junius_brutus|Lucius Junius Brutus]] is a Greek-style tyrant narrative. Yet the city the Tarquins left behind was formidable. The Capitoline temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, dedicated according to tradition in the Republic's first year, stood on a podium of roughly 60 by 50 metres, as large as any temple in the Greek world. The first treaty with Carthage, which Polybius (3.22) read on bronze and dated to the first consuls, shows Rome claiming to speak for the Latin coastal towns of Ardea, Antium, Circeii and Tarracina. A Rome that negotiated with Carthage on those terms was a regional power, not a village. The fifth century, by contrast, shows a sharp fall in imported Greek pottery and temple building across Latium: an economic recession, compounded by pressure from the hill peoples.

The new state replaced the king with two annually elected magistrates holding imperium, later called consuls (originally perhaps praetores, as the 'praetor maximus' of an old law on driving a nail suggests). They were checked by collegiality and the one-year term, and in emergencies superseded by a dictator for six months. The Senate advised; the comitia centuriata, the people organised in property classes and age groups as an army, elected magistrates and declared war. Religion was bound into every public act: no assembly met and no battle was joined without taking the auspices, and the major priesthoods, pontiffs and augurs, were held by the same men who held office.

The central domestic theme of the next century and a half is what the Romans called the conflict of the orders. The patricians were a hereditary group of families who monopolised the priesthoods and, Livy says, the consulship. But the early fasti contain plebeian names (Junius, Cassius, Genucius, Sempronius), which suggests that the patriciate hardened into a closed caste during the fifth century rather than existing from the start. The plebs was not a single class: it included rich families excluded from honours as well as poor peasants threatened with debt bondage (nexum), land hunger and arbitrary treatment by magistrates. These different grievances explain why the movement both persisted and eventually split.

The plebs' weapon was secession. In 494 they withdrew from the city (to the Sacred Mount or the Aventine) and swore a collective oath (lex sacrata) to treat as accursed anyone who harmed their chosen leaders, the tribunes of the plebs. Around the tribunes grew a parallel organisation, a 'state within the state' in Arnaldo Momigliano's phrase: plebeian aediles who looked after the temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine (vowed 496, dedicated 493), and a plebeian assembly that from 471 (lex Publilia Voleronis) voted by tribes. The tribune's power was negative and personal: he could intervene physically to protect a citizen from a magistrate (auxilium) and later veto public business (intercessio).

The demand for published law produced the Twelve Tables, drafted by two boards of ten (decemviri legibus scribundis) in 451-450. Their fragments, quoted by later jurists and antiquarians, give the clearest picture of fifth-century society we possess. They regulate summons to court, the seizure and, if creditors insisted, the division of an insolvent debtor ('partes secanto'), the power of the father (a son sold three times went free), inheritance, damage to crops, the patron who cheats his client ('sacer esto'), and lavish funerals. This was a world of peasant households, slaves, clients and kin groups (gentes). The second decemvirate's alleged tyranny and the death of Verginia are melodrama; but the ban on intermarriage between patricians and plebeians was real enough to be repealed by the lex Canuleia of 445. The Valerio-Horatian laws of 449, which supposedly made plebiscites binding on all, are almost certainly an anticipation of the lex Hortensia of 287.

From 444 to 367 the state was often headed not by consuls but by military tribunes with consular power, three, four, and eventually six at a time. Livy explains them as a compromise allowing plebeians into the chief magistracy, yet no plebeian is clearly attested until Publius Licinius Calvus in 400. The rising number of colleges in years of multiple wars favours the view that the office answered a military need for more commanders with imperium. Both factors probably operated.

War shaped everything. After the battle of [[battle_of_lake_regillus|Lake Regillus]] (496) the foedus Cassianum of 493 bound Rome and the Latin League in a defensive alliance with shared booty and joint colonies. Through the fifth century the Aequi and Volsci, highland peoples pushing into the plains, raided Latium almost annually, which is the context for the Cincinnatus legend ([[cincinnatus|Cincinnatus]]). Warfare was still partly clan-based: the 306 Fabii who died on the Cremera in 477 fought as a private army, and the Lapis Satricanus, an inscription of about 500 BC, records a dedication to Mars by the 'companions' (suodales) of one Poplios Valesios, plausibly Publius Valerius Poplicola. The decisive step was the war with Veii, the Etruscan city 15 km north across the Tiber. Its capture by [[marcus_furius_camillus|Camillus]] in 396, after a siege the annalists stretched to ten years on the Trojan model, nearly doubled Roman territory. To sustain long campaigns, pay for soldiers (stipendium) was introduced in 406, financed by a direct property tax (tributum).

Within a few years came catastrophe. A Gallic war band, probably Senones on a raid southward, routed the Roman army at the [[battle_of_allia|Allia]] and sacked the city (Varronian 390; 387/386 by Greek reckoning). The ransom of a thousand pounds of gold and [[brennus|Brennus]]' 'vae victis' entered legend, as did the apologetic tale of Camillus' last-minute rescue. The damage to Rome's power was short-lived. Within a generation the Romans had built a circuit wall of over 11 km in Grotta Oscura tufa quarried in the territory of Veii, founded colonies at Sutrium and Nepet, created four new rural tribes on the Veientine land (387), and incorporated Tusculum as a community of citizens (381).

The internal settlement came with the Licinian-Sextian laws of 367, carried after years of obstruction by the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius. They opened the consulship to plebeians (Sextius was first, in 366), limited holdings of public land to 500 iugera (a figure many think was retrojected from the Gracchan age), and relieved debtors. The praetorship and curule aedileship were created in 366, and the keepers of the Sibylline books were enlarged to ten, half plebeian. The result was not democracy but a new governing class: a patricio-plebeian nobility defined by office-holding rather than birth, which would rule Rome for the next three centuries.
chapters.historiography: The basic question is how much of the annalistic tradition can be trusted. Hypercritical scholars (Alföldi, von Ungern-Sternberg, Forsythe) see the fifth century as largely reconstructed by late-Republican writers projecting their own politics backward; Cornell defends a core of authentic documentary data, including the fasti and the Twelve Tables. Archaeology since the 1970s (the 'Grande Roma dei Tarquini' exhibition, Satricum, the Regia and Comitium excavations) supports a large, wealthy archaic city and a fifth-century downturn. On the Struggle of the Orders, the Raaflaub volume framed debate: whether the patriciate closed only in the fifth century (Momigliano, Cornell), whether the plebs originated as a client class or a mass excluded by that closure (Richard), and whether the consular tribunate was a political or military device. Forsythe and Bradley stress that the narrative of a single, linear conflict is itself a construction of later historians who saw the Gracchi in the tribunes of 494.

chapters.title: The Conquest of Italy
chapters.body:
Between the Licinian-Sextian laws and the first crossing to Sicily, Rome went from being one Latin city among many to the master of peninsular Italy south of the Po valley. Its territory grew from perhaps 2,000 to about 27,000 square kilometres of citizen land, with a network of allies covering roughly 100,000 more. How and why this happened is one of the great problems of ancient history, because the mechanism Rome created in these decades, a permanent alliance system yielding manpower rather than tribute, was the engine of everything that followed.

The decisive institutional innovation came after the Latin War of 340-338. The Latins, allies under the foedus Cassianum, revolted against Roman dominance and were defeated, with the aid of Campanian cavalry, in battles near Vesuvius (where Livy places the self-sacrifice, devotio, of the consul Publius Decius Mus) and at Trifanum. The settlement of 338 dissolved the League and treated each community separately. Some, such as Lanuvium, Aricia and Nomentum, were incorporated as municipia of full citizens. Others, including Capua, Fundi and Formiae, received citizenship without the vote (civitas sine suffragio), bearing military and fiscal burdens while governing themselves. Tibur and Praeneste remained allies; Antium's fleet was destroyed and the bronze beaks of its ships fixed to the speakers' platform in the Forum, which took the name Rostra. The genius of the system lay in its flexibility: graded statuses, bilateral treaties, and the promise of promotion bound communities to Rome individually and prevented them combining.

Colonisation was the second instrument. 'Latin' colonies, settlements of several thousand families with Latin rights and their own magistrates, were planted at strategic nodes: Cales (334), Fregellae (328), Luceria (314), Alba Fucens (303, 6,000 settlers), Venusia (291, reportedly 20,000). Small citizen colonies of 300 families guarded the coast at Antium, Tarracina and later Minturnae and Sinuessa. Each colony took land from the defeated, gave it to Roman and Latin peasants, and created a garrison that was also a recruiting ground. Roads connected them: the Via Appia, built by the censor [[appius_claudius_caecus|Appius Claudius Caecus]] in 312, ran some 195 km (132 Roman miles) from Rome to Capua with long straight stretches across the Pomptine marshes.

The Samnites, a confederation of Oscan-speaking highland peoples in the central and southern Apennines, were Rome's hardest opponents. The [[first_samnite_war|First Samnite War]] (343-341), triggered by Capua's surrender to Rome to obtain protection, is so poorly reported that some historians doubt it happened in the form Livy gives. The [[second_samnite_war|Second Samnite War]] (326-304) began over Naples and the colony at Fregellae. In 321 both consular armies were trapped in a defile at the Caudine Forks and sent under the yoke; the peace that followed was disowned by the Senate according to Livy, who probably invented the swift revenge he describes. Rome recovered by encircling Samnium with colonies and alliances in Apulia and Lucania, and by reorganising its army: the manipular legion, with its flexible lines of maniples and the javelin (pilum) and oblong shield (scutum), is often attributed to lessons learned in these mountain wars. A second legion pair appears around 311, giving four legions annually.

The [[third_samnite_war|Third Samnite War]] (298-290) became a general Italian war. Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls combined, and in 295 met Rome at [[battle_of_sentinum|Sentinum]] in Umbria, the largest battle fought in Italy to that date. Decius Mus the younger repeated his father's devotio; the Greek historian Duris of Samos put enemy dead at 100,000, an inflated figure that nonetheless shows the battle was known in the Greek world. The epitaph of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus (consul 298), carved on his sarcophagus in the family tomb on the Via Appia, boasts of taking Taurasia and Cisauna and subduing Lucania, and is the oldest Roman historical text in verse. In 290 [[manius_curius_dentatus|Manius Curius Dentatus]] conquered the Sabines, who received citizenship without the vote, and ended the Samnite resistance. The Senones were expelled from the ager Gallicus on the Adriatic in 283-282 and a colony planted at Sena Gallica.

Domestic politics adjusted to conquest. The leges Publiliae of 339 required one censor to be plebeian and weakened the Senate's control over legislation; the lex Poetelia Papiria (326 or 313) abolished debt bondage, which became unnecessary once war supplied slaves and land; the lex Ogulnia of 300 opened the priesthoods of pontiffs and augurs to plebeians. Appius Claudius' censorship of 312 was controversial: he distributed the landless across all the tribes, enrolled sons of freedmen in the Senate and built the first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia. In 304 his client Gnaeus Flavius, a freedman's son and curule aedile, published the forms of legal action and the calendar of court days, ending pontifical control of legal knowledge. The final secession of 287 led to the lex Hortensia, making the resolutions of the plebeian assembly binding on the whole people. Formally the conflict of the orders was over.

The Greek cities of the south completed the picture. Tarentum, the richest, had long hired condottieri from mainland Greece. When Rome garrisoned Thurii and sent ships into the Gulf of Tarentum in 282, apparently breaching an older agreement, the Tarentines sank them and called in [[pyrrhus|Pyrrhus]], king of Epirus and one of the most talented generals of the Hellenistic age. In the [[pyrrhic_war|Pyrrhic War]] (280-275) he won at [[battle_of_heraclea|Heraclea]] (280), using elephants for the first time against Romans, and at [[battle_of_asculum|Asculum]] (279), but at a cost that made his name proverbial. His ambassador Cineas reportedly called the Senate an assembly of kings, and the blind Appius Claudius Caecus spoke against negotiation in a speech still read in Cicero's day. What defeated Pyrrhus was manpower: Roman losses were replaced from the reservoir of citizens and allies, his were not. After a Sicilian adventure against Carthage he returned and was checked at [[battle_of_beneventum|Beneventum]] (then called Maleventum, 275). Tarentum surrendered in 272, Rhegium was retaken from its mutinous Campanian garrison in 270, and Volsinii, the last independent Etruscan power of note, was destroyed in 264.

Why did Rome expand so relentlessly? The ancient answer was virtue and divine favour. William Harris argued that war was structural: the aristocracy's competition for glory, the peasantry's appetite for land and booty, and an annual rhythm of campaigning made it the normal state of affairs. Arthur Eckstein replied that Rome was no more aggressive than its neighbours in a militarised, anarchic world of states, and that its distinctive feature was its ability to incorporate allies. Both views agree that the alliance system was decisive: the allies paid no tribute but furnished troops, and in return shared booty and land and Roman protection. Each successful war therefore made the next one easier to fight, and there was little in the structure to tell the system to stop.

By 264 Rome commanded a confederation that Polybius' manpower list of 225, drawn from Fabius Pictor, counts at some 700,000 infantry and 70,000 cavalry of military age. It had a common military obligation, a capital that had begun to coin silver (the Romano-Campanian didrachms), a nobility of consular families such as the Fabii, Valerii, Cornelii and Decii, and a habit of victory. It was about to be tested against a sea power.
chapters.historiography: Debate centres on the causes and character of expansion. Harris's War and Imperialism (1979) made Roman aggression structural and deliberate; Eckstein's realist reading (2006) and Rich's 'fear, greed and glory' essay stress the competitive interstate system and defensive motives. Terrenato (2019) recasts conquest as a negotiated process among Italian elites with shared interests, minimising the narrative of violent subjugation. The reliability of Livy's account of the Samnite wars (Oakley's commentary is fundamental), the date and nature of the manipular reform, and the legal status of civitas sine suffragio (originally an honour or a burden?) remain contested, as does the extent to which the 'Roman Confederation' was a coherent system rather than an accretion of ad hoc deals.
reading: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X (1997-2005)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome 327-70 BC (1979)
Eckstein, Mediterranean Anarchy, Interstate War, and the Rise of Rome (2006)
Terrenato, The Early Roman Expansion into Italy (2019)
Fronda, Between Rome and Carthage (2010)

chapters.title: Rome and Carthage
chapters.body:
Carthage in 264 was the greatest power of the western Mediterranean: a Phoenician city of perhaps 100,000 or more inhabitants, ruling the fertile hinterland of modern Tunisia, a chain of trading posts from Libya to the Atlantic, Sardinia, and the western half of Sicily. It was governed by two annual suffetes, a council and a court of 104, with an assembly that mattered more than Roman writers liked to admit. Its armies were mostly mercenaries and subject levies commanded by citizen generals; its strength was money and a navy of quinqueremes. Rome and Carthage had concluded treaties in 509, 348 and 279/278, the last against Pyrrhus. The [[first_punic_war|First Punic War]] began over the small city of Messana, held by Campanian mercenaries, the Mamertines, who appealed to both powers against Hiero II of Syracuse. Polybius (1.10-11) reports that the Senate hesitated and the people, tempted by booty, voted for war. The consul Appius Claudius Caudex crossed the straits in 264.

The war lasted twenty-three years and transformed Rome into a naval power. In 261 the Romans built a fleet of 100 quinqueremes, reportedly copying a stranded Carthaginian ship, and trained rowers on benches ashore. To negate Punic seamanship they fitted a boarding bridge with a spike, the corvus, and in 260 Gaius Duilius won at [[battle_of_mylae|Mylae]]. In 256, at [[battle_of_ecnomus|Ecnomus]], about 330 Roman ships met some 350 Carthaginian, perhaps 290,000 men in all, in one of the largest naval battles in history. The invasion of Africa that followed ended in disaster when Marcus Atilius Regulus was defeated by the Spartan mercenary Xanthippus in 255; the story of his parole and torture is a later moral fable. Storms did more damage than the enemy: in 255 off Camarina some 284 of 364 ships were wrecked, in 253 another 150, and the corvus may have made ships top-heavy. At [[battle_of_drepana|Drepana]] in 249 Publius Claudius Pulcher, after throwing overboard the sacred chickens that refused to eat ('let them drink'), lost 93 ships. On land the war settled into sieges of Lilybaeum and Drepana and guerrilla warfare against [[hamilcar_barca|Hamilcar Barca]] on Mount Eryx. The decision came only when wealthy Romans lent the state money for a final fleet of 200 ships, to be repaid after victory. Gaius Lutatius Catulus destroyed the Carthaginian relief fleet off the [[battle_of_aegates_islands|Aegates Islands]] in March 241. Carthage evacuated Sicily and paid 3,200 talents over ten years.

Victory created the first provinces. Sicily, apart from Hiero's kingdom, was placed under a Roman magistrate; Rome seized Sardinia and Corsica in 238 while Carthage was fighting its own unpaid mercenaries (the Truceless War), and extorted another 1,200 talents. In 227 two additional praetors were created to govern Sicily and Sardinia. The province was at first simply a magistrate's sphere of command (provincia); the apparatus of tribute collection, inherited in Sicily from Hiero's tithe law (lex Hieronica), came to define it. Polybius saw the seizure of Sardinia as the real cause of the second war, because it convinced the Barcid family that Rome could not be trusted.

Hamilcar went to Spain in 237, taking his nine-year-old son [[hannibal_barca|Hannibal]] after the famous oath of enmity. Over the next eighteen years Hamilcar, his son-in-law [[hasdrubal_the_fair|Hasdrubal]] and Hannibal built a Punic empire in southern and eastern Iberia, with silver mines near New Carthage (Cartagena) yielding, Pliny says, 300 pounds a day at Baebelo. Rome's Ebro treaty with Hasdrubal (226 or 225) set a limit to Punic expansion. Hannibal's siege of Saguntum, a city south of the Ebro with some Roman connection, gave Rome its casus belli in 219-218. The legal questions that absorbed ancient writers (was Saguntum protected by treaty? was the Ebro treaty binding on Carthage?) matter less than the fact that both powers were prepared to fight.

Hannibal's strategy in the [[second_punic_war|Second Punic War]] was audacious: to invade Italy by land, avoiding Roman naval superiority, and break the alliance system by detaching the allies. He left New Carthage in spring 218 with perhaps 90,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry, crossed the Pyrenees, the Rhône and the Alps (the pass is still disputed), and reached the Po valley with about 26,000 men and a handful of elephants. Within twenty months he destroyed three Roman armies: at the [[battle_of_trebia|Trebia]] (December 218), at [[battle_of_lake_trasimene|Lake Trasimene]] (June 217), where the consul Gaius Flaminius died in an ambush in the morning mist, and at [[battle_of_cannae|Cannae]] (2 August 216). At Cannae an army of about 86,000 was enveloped and between 50,000 and 70,000 killed, including the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus and some eighty senators. The tactical masterpiece, Hannibal's double envelopment with a deliberately yielding centre of Gauls and Spaniards, has been studied in staff colleges ever since.

The political result was partial. Capua, the second city of Italy, defected, as did much of Samnium, Apulia, Lucania and Bruttium, and later Tarentum. Philip V of Macedon allied with Hannibal in 215, and Syracuse defected after Hiero's death. Yet the Latin colonies and the core of central Italy held, and Rome refused to negotiate. Under the delaying strategy associated with [[quintus_fabius_maximus|Quintus Fabius Maximus]], 'Cunctator', the Romans avoided pitched battle with Hannibal, kept up to 25 legions in the field, and wore down his allies. Marcus Claudius Marcellus ([[marcus_claudius_marcellus|Marcellus]]) took Syracuse in 212 despite Archimedes' engines. Capua fell in 211 even after Hannibal's march to the gates of Rome; its senators were executed and its land confiscated as Roman public land. The cost at home was ruinous: the property tax doubled, the coinage collapsed and was replaced around 211 by the new silver denarius, slaves were enrolled as volunteers (volones), and in 209 twelve of the thirty Latin colonies declared they could give no more men.

The war was decided in Spain and Africa. Publius and Gnaeus Scipio held the Ebro line until their deaths in 211. Their son and nephew, the young Publius Cornelius Scipio ([[scipio_africanus|Scipio Africanus]]), given proconsular command as a private citizen aged about twenty-five, captured New Carthage in 209 in a daring assault across a lagoon, and destroyed Carthaginian power in Iberia at Ilipa (206). [[hasdrubal_barca|Hasdrubal Barca]], marching to reinforce his brother, was caught and killed at the [[battle_of_metaurus|Metaurus]] in 207 after the consul Gaius Claudius Nero's forced march from Apulia. In 204 Scipio invaded Africa, allied with the Numidian prince [[masinissa|Masinissa]], burned the enemy camps and won at the Great Plains. Hannibal, recalled after sixteen years in Italy, was defeated at [[battle_of_zama|Zama]] in 202, where Scipio's open lanes channelled the elephants and the Numidian and Italian cavalry decided the day.

The peace of 201 left Carthage independent but crippled: an indemnity of 10,000 talents over fifty years, a fleet of ten triremes, and no right to make war without Roman permission. Rome emerged with two Spanish provinces (formalised in 197), dominance over Italy reinforced by confiscations from the defectors, a battle-hardened citizen army, a much larger Senate-dominated state apparatus, and commanders like Scipio whose personal prestige was a portent. The fear of Hannibal never quite left Roman political culture.
chapters.historiography: Polybius, who knew Scipio Aemilianus and interviewed survivors, is the backbone of modern accounts; Livy's third decade adds much detail of uneven value. Debate turns on war guilt (the Saguntum and Ebro questions, Hoyos's 'unplanned wars'), on Hannibal's strategy (did he aim to destroy Rome or merely reduce it to a regional power within a new balance?), on Fabius' strategy and the role of the Senate, and on the loyalty of the allies (Fronda shows that local rivalries, more than attitudes to Rome, determined defection). The scale of Roman mobilisation, perhaps 10 per cent or more of the free population under arms, underpins Brunt's demographic analysis. Proctor's and Lancel's work on the Alpine route and Carthaginian society, and recent excavations at Carthage, have reduced the Romanocentric bias of the sources somewhat.
reading: Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998)
Fronda, Between Rome and Carthage (2010)

chapters.title: The Imperial Republic: Government, Economy and Society
chapters.body:
Polybius devoted the sixth book of his Histories to the Roman constitution, because he believed it explained Rome's success. He saw a mixture of monarchy (the consuls), aristocracy (the Senate) and democracy (the assemblies), each checking the others, held together by religious awe and an ethic of service exemplified by the aristocratic funeral, where actors wearing the wax masks (imagines) of a man's ancestors rode in procession and his son recounted their deeds from the Rostra. The picture is idealised but not wrong. The Roman state of the middle Republic had no bureaucracy to speak of: a few dozen annual magistrates, a Senate of about 300 former magistrates who served for life, and assemblies that met when summoned. It ran an empire through these men, their households and the contractors they hired.

Office-holding was competitive and hierarchical. The lex Villia annalis of 180 fixed minimum ages and intervals between offices; the cursus ran from military service through the quaestorship and aedileship to the praetorship (six a year from 197) and the consulship. The nobility, the families with consular ancestors, monopolised the top office: of 200 consuls between 200 and 101 BC, only a handful were 'new men' like [[cato_the_elder|Marcus Porcius Cato]] (consul 195). Electoral success depended on reputation, wealth, family networks and favours, but the voters were not sheep. Elections in the centuriate assembly were weighted towards the propertied, and the urban poor were confined to four of the thirty-five tribes, yet results were often unpredictable, and Fergus Millar's insistence that the people's sovereignty was real, not decorative, has reshaped the debate. The censors, elected every five years, counted citizens and property, revised the Senate list, and let the great public contracts.

Empire brought money on an unprecedented scale. Indemnities from Carthage (10,000 talents) and Antiochus (15,000), booty from Macedon and Asia, provincial tributes, and the Spanish silver mines (where Polybius says 40,000 workers produced 25,000 drachmas a day near New Carthage) flowed into the treasury and into private hands. Aemilius Paullus' triumph in 167 deposited so much that the citizen property tax was suspended for good. The state spent it on armies, roads, aqueducts (the Aqua Marcia of 144-140 cost 180 million sesterces according to Frontinus) and the transformation of the city. Basilicas appeared in the Forum (Porcia 184, Aemilia 179, Sempronia 169), and the Emporium and Porticus Aemilia below the Aventine (193) handled imports through the river port. Contractors, the publicani, organised in companies (societates) and drawn from the equestrian order, built, supplied and collected.

The second great import was people. Wars produced captives on a vast scale: 25,000 from Agrigentum in 261, 30,000 from Tarentum in 209, 150,000 from Epirus in 167, 50,000 from Carthage in 146. Keith Hopkins argued that Rome's conquests and the transformation of Italian agriculture were linked in a single cycle: the rich invested booty in land, bought out or displaced smallholders who were absent on long campaigns, and worked the new estates with slaves. Cato's handbook On Agriculture (c. 160) describes such an estate: an olive grove of 240 iugera worked by a bailiff and a staff of 13, a vineyard of 100 iugera by 16, with instructions to sell old slaves and worn-out oxen. By the end of the Republic Italy may have contained between one and three million slaves, a slave society in the full sense, and the first great slave revolt broke out in Sicily around 136.

How far smallholders actually disappeared is disputed. The Gracchan narrative, transmitted by Appian and Plutarch, holds that the peasantry was squeezed off the land by slave estates and that the census of citizens fell (from 337,022 in 164 to 317,933 in 136), threatening the recruiting base. Revisionists (Rosenstein, de Ligt) note that the archaeological surveys of Italian countryside show continued small farms in many regions, that the falling census may reflect evasion, and that population growth, not decline, may have created land hunger. The tension between these models is central to understanding the crisis that followed in 133.

The allies were the hidden casualties of success. They provided as many soldiers as the Romans, often more, but received a smaller share of booty, and from the 170s the Senate allotted them smaller plots in colonies. Latins migrating to Rome were expelled in 187 and 177. Gaius Gracchus later told the story of a consul who had the chief magistrate of Teanum Sidicinum stripped and flogged in the forum because the men's baths had not been cleared fast enough for his wife (Gellius 10.3). Such grievances fed the demand for citizenship that exploded in 91.

Religion was public, civic and adaptable. Generals vowed temples in battle and built them from booty, so the temples of Rome form a map of its wars. In crises the Senate consulted the Sibylline books, which prescribed new rites: the lectisternium of twelve gods in 217, and in 205-204 the summoning of the Magna Mater, the black stone of Cybele, from Pessinus in Phrygia, received by Publius Scipio Nasica as the best man in the state and installed on the Palatine. In 228, 216 and 114 a Gallic and a Greek couple were buried alive in the Forum Boarium, a rite Livy calls 'hardly Roman'. Religion was also policed. In 186 the Senate suppressed the Bacchic cult in Italy, allegedly implicating 7,000 people; the bronze copy of its decree found at Tiriolo in Bruttium (the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus) shows it allowing small, supervised gatherings while destroying the cult's organisation. The danger perceived was not doctrine but an association outside the control of magistrates and fathers.

Contact with Greek culture transformed Roman literature and self-image. Latin literature began in 240 with a play translated from Greek by Livius Andronicus, a freedman from Tarentum. Naevius wrote an epic on the First Punic War; Ennius, from Calabria, wrote the Annales, a hexameter history of Rome; Plautus adapted Greek New Comedy for Roman audiences with Roman jokes, and Terence more faithfully. The first Roman historians wrote in Greek for a Greek readership; Cato's Origines was the first history in Latin. Cato's hostility to Greek doctors and philosophers was performative: he learned Greek and used Greek sources. In 155 the Athenian embassy of three philosophers lectured in Rome; Carneades argued for justice one day and against it the next. Scholars once spoke of a 'Scipionic circle' of philhellenes around Aemilianus, Polybius and the Stoic Panaetius; the label is modern, but the intellectual exchange was real. Erich Gruen has argued that Romans used Hellenism to define, not dilute, a Roman identity.

Women of the elite gained wealth and visibility with empire. The lex Oppia of 215, a wartime limit on women's gold and coloured clothing, was repealed in 195 after women demonstrated in the Forum, despite Cato. The lex Voconia of 169 barred women from being named heirs to the largest estates, which suggests how much property they were acquiring through inheritance and marriage without manus. Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus and mother of the Gracchi, became the model of the educated Roman matrona; her letters were still read in Cicero's day.

By 133 the Republic had grown an empire while keeping the institutions of a city-state. Its governing class was richer and more competitive than ever, its armies served longer and further away, its countryside was changing, its allies were restless, and the plebs of the capital was growing. None of this made revolution inevitable. It made the political system dangerously dependent on the restraint of men who had increasing reason not to exercise it.
chapters.historiography: Two debates dominate. On politics, the twentieth-century model of an oligarchy run by family factions and patronage (Münzer, Scullard, Syme) gave way to Millar's argument that the Republic had a genuinely democratic element in its assemblies and contiones; Hölkeskamp, Mouritsen and Morstein-Marx counter that popular participation was ritualised consensus within an aristocratic political culture. On the economy, Hopkins's model of conquest, slavery and peasant displacement (building on Toynbee's Hannibal's Legacy and Brunt's Italian Manpower) has been challenged by survey archaeology, by debates over the 'low count' versus 'high count' of the Augustan census (which implies very different population trajectories), and by de Ligt's and Rosenstein's arguments that land shortage arose from population growth. The scale and organisation of slavery remain contested, as does the degree of market integration.

chapters.title: Rome and the Greek East
chapters.body:
Within fifty-three years, as Polybius put it in the opening of his Histories, almost the whole inhabited world fell under Roman rule. He wrote as a Greek hostage in Rome after 167 and wanted to explain how. His answer combined the Roman constitution, the discipline of the army and the moral cohesion of the governing class. Modern historians add an analysis of the Hellenistic state system the Romans entered, a world of three great monarchies (Antigonid Macedon, Seleucid Asia, Ptolemaic Egypt), middling powers such as Pergamum and Rhodes, and federal leagues of Greek cities (Aetolian, Achaean) locked in competition.

The first contacts were Adriatic. In the [[first_illyrian_war|First Illyrian War]] (229-228) Rome suppressed the piracy of Queen Teuta's subjects, taking Corcyra, Apollonia and Epidamnus into its protection. The Second Illyrian War (219) expelled Demetrius of Pharos, who fled to Philip V of Macedon ([[philip_v|Philip V]]). Philip's treaty with Hannibal in 215 brought the [[first_macedonian_war|First Macedonian War]] (214-205), fought cheaply by Rome through an alliance with the Aetolians (211), whose terms (Rome takes movable booty and captives, Aetolia the land and cities) survive on an inscription from Thyrrheion. It ended in a compromise peace at Phoenice.

The [[second_macedonian_war|Second Macedonian War]] (200-197) is the classic test case for Roman motives. In 201 Pergamene and Rhodian envoys reported that Philip and the Seleucid Antiochus III ([[antiochus_iii|Antiochus III]]) had made a pact to partition the overseas possessions of the child-king Ptolemy V. The centuriate assembly first voted against war, exhausted after Hannibal, and had to be persuaded. Was the Senate moved by fear of a resurgent Macedon, by obligations to friends, by desire for glory and booty, or by resentment of Philip's earlier alliance with Hannibal? The war was won by Titus Quinctius Flamininus, consul at about thirty, who defeated Philip at [[battle_of_cynoscephalae|Cynoscephalae]] in Thessaly in 197, a battle famous for the legion's flexibility against the phalanx on broken ground. At the Isthmian Games of 196 he proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks, and in 194 Roman troops left Greece entirely. The slogan was sincere propaganda: Rome would leave Greek cities self-governing, ungarrisoned and free of tribute, but would expect them to behave as grateful clients.

Antiochus III, who had rebuilt Seleucid power from Bactria to the Aegean in a famous anabasis, crossed into Thrace and then, at the Aetolians' invitation, into Greece in 192. He gave refuge to Hannibal. Defeated at Thermopylae in 191 (where Cato led a flanking march along the path of the Persians of 480), he was pursued into Asia by Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his brother Africanus as legate, and crushed at [[battle_of_magnesia|Magnesia]] in late 190 or early 189. The peace of Apamea (188) excluded him from Asia Minor west of the Taurus, took his elephants and fleet, and imposed 15,000 talents, then the largest indemnity in history. Rome kept no territory: Pergamum and Rhodes were enlarged instead. Gnaeus Manlius Vulso's unprovoked campaign against the Galatians in 189 and the booty he brought home became for later moralists the moment when Asian luxury entered Rome.

The third war against Macedon showed the system hardening. Philip's son Perseus revived Macedonian influence among Greek cities and in Thrace, married a Seleucid princess, and courted the poor of Greece with debt relief. Eumenes II of Pergamum denounced him at Rome in 172; an assassination attempt on Eumenes at Delphi was blamed on Perseus. The [[third_macedonian_war|Third Macedonian War]] (171-168) began badly for Rome but ended at [[battle_of_pydna|Pydna]] on 22 June 168 (a lunar eclipse on the night before allows the precise date), when Lucius Aemilius Paullus broke the phalanx on uneven ground. The Antigonid monarchy was abolished and Macedon divided into four republics paying half the old royal taxes. In Epirus, on Senate orders, Paullus sacked seventy towns and enslaved 150,000 people in a day. A thousand Achaean notables, Polybius among them, were deported to Italy. Rhodes, suspected of sympathy for Perseus, lost its mainland possessions and was ruined when Delos was made a free port. In the same summer, at Eleusis outside Alexandria, the envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the sand round Antiochus IV and demanded an answer before he stepped out of it: the king withdrew from Egypt. From 167 the tributum on Roman citizens was suspended, paid for by eastern wealth.

In the West, war in Spain was continuous and harder. Two provinces were created in 197; Cato as consul in 195 campaigned in the north-east and organised the silver mines. Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus' settlement of 179, with fair treaties and tribute, bought a generation of relative peace. From 154 the Lusitanian and Celtiberian wars resumed with a brutality that shocked contemporaries: Servius Sulpicius Galba massacred thousands of Lusitanians who had surrendered (150), and the shepherd Viriathus led a resistance until his murder by bribed companions in 139. The Celtiberian hill town of Numantia defeated a series of commanders and forced Gaius Hostilius Mancinus to a treaty (137) that the Senate disowned, handing Mancinus over naked to the enemy. Levies for Spain became so unpopular that tribunes imprisoned consuls in 151 and 138. The consular year was moved to begin on 1 January from 153 so that commanders could reach Spain in time to campaign.

The year 146 marked the end of the Hellenistic balance. A pretender, Andriscus, claiming to be Perseus' son, reunited Macedonia in 149-148 and was defeated by Quintus Caecilius Metellus; Macedonia became a province. In 146 the Achaean League, provoked by Roman interference in its quarrel with Sparta, went to war and was destroyed; Lucius Mummius sacked Corinth, killed its men, sold its women and children, and shipped its art to Italy. In the same year Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus ([[scipio_aemilianus|Scipio Aemilianus]]) destroyed Carthage after a three-year siege. The [[third_punic_war|Third Punic War]] (149-146) had been engineered by Cato's party, who exploited Carthage's breach of the 201 treaty when it defended itself against Masinissa's encroachments; the Carthaginians surrendered their arms and then were told to abandon their city and move ten miles inland. Africa became a province. Scipio Aemilianus then took Numantia in 133 after a siege behind 9 km of circumvallation. In the same year Attalus III bequeathed Pergamum to the Roman people.

Polybius identified a shift after Pydna from hegemony to command, from 'friends' to subjects. Modern scholars debate how far Rome sought formal empire. Until 146 it annexed reluctantly in the East, preferring indirect control through obligations of friendship (amicitia) and patronage, backed by the threat of the legions. Its decisions were made in the Senate by a few hundred men, reacting to embassies, honour and opportunity, and the decisions of any given year can look improvised. But the cumulative result, by 133, was an empire on which the Senate and people of Rome depended for revenue, slaves, land and status. Its effects at home are the subject of the next chapter.
chapters.historiography: The 'defensive imperialism' thesis of Mommsen, Holleaux and Badian (Rome expanded to protect itself and its clients, annexing only when forced) was challenged by Harris (aggressive, economically and socially driven expansion) and refined by Gruen, who argued that the Greeks drew the Romans in and that Roman diplomacy adapted Hellenistic norms rather than imposing Roman patron-client categories. Eckstein's realist account emphasises a 'power-transition crisis' in the East after 207 as the Ptolemaic state weakened. Kallet-Marx dates the true transition to provincial rule in the East to the Mithridatic era rather than 146. Spain, studied by Richardson, shows a quite different, more violent mode of expansion, and complicates generalisations based on Greece.
reading: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Badian, Foreign Clientelae 264-70 BC (1958)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Richardson, Hispaniae: Spain and the Development of Roman Imperialism (1986)
Errington, The Dawn of Empire (1972)

chapters.title: From the Gracchi to Sulla
chapters.body:
Ancient writers from Sallust to Appian agreed that the Republic's decline began in 133 with the tribunate of [[tiberius_gracchus|Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus]]. A nobleman of the highest birth, grandson of Scipio Africanus, he had served at Carthage and Numantia and had negotiated the disowned treaty of 137. His agrarian law reasserted the old limit of 500 iugera on holdings of public land (with 250 more for each of two sons), confiscated the excess and distributed it in small inalienable plots to poor citizens, administered by a board of three. The proposal was legal and backed by eminent senators. What made it explosive was Gracchus' method. When his fellow tribune Marcus Octavius vetoed the bill, Gracchus had the assembly depose him, an unprecedented act. When the Senate refused funds, he proposed using the treasure of Attalus III, just bequeathed to Rome, encroaching on the Senate's control of finance and foreign affairs. When he stood for re-election, his enemies saw a would-be king. On election day the pontifex maximus Publius Scipio Nasica led a crowd of senators and their followers who clubbed Gracchus and some 300 supporters to death; their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. It was, said Plutarch, the first civil strife at Rome since the expulsion of the kings to end in bloodshed.

The land commission survived its founder. Boundary stones inscribed with the commissioners' names (the cippi Gracchani) have been found in Campania, Lucania and Apulia, and the citizen census jumped from 318,823 in 131 to 394,736 in 125, perhaps because new smallholders now qualified. But the reclaimed land was often held by Italian allies, whose protests found a patron in Scipio Aemilianus; his sudden death in 129 was rumoured to be murder. The consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus proposed citizenship for the allies in 125; the revolt and destruction of the Latin colony of Fregellae that year showed what was at stake.

[[gaius_gracchus|Gaius Gracchus]], tribune in 123 and 122, had a broader programme. His grain law provided a monthly ration to citizens at a fixed subsidised price; his judiciary law transferred the jury of the extortion court from senators to equites; his law on Asia had the province's tithes auctioned in Rome, delivering its taxpayers to the companies of the publicani; he built roads and granaries and planned colonies, including Junonia on the cursed site of Carthage. His proposal to give citizenship to Latins and Latin rights to other allies failed, undercut by the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus, who outbid him with promises he never intended to keep. In 121 the Senate, for the first time, passed its 'last decree' (senatus consultum ultimum) urging the consuls to see that the state came to no harm. The consul Lucius Opimius used Cretan archers to storm the Aventine; Gracchus had himself killed by a slave, and some 3,000 of his followers were executed. Opimius then rebuilt the temple of Concord. Someone scrawled on it that discord had built the temple of Concord.

The Gracchi left a repertoire rather than a party. Later politicians who worked through the tribunate and the assemblies and appealed to the people's interests (grain, land, the ballot, the courts) were called populares; their opponents, defenders of senatorial authority, called themselves optimates, the best men. These were styles of politics adopted by members of the same elite, not ideological organisations, and the same man could change sides.

Foreign failure exposed the governing class. In Numidia [[jugurtha|Jugurtha]], Masinissa's grandson, eliminated his cousins, massacred Italian traders at Cirta (112), and survived by bribing Roman commanders and envoys; Sallust's monograph made him the symbol of a venal Senate. In the north, migrating Germanic peoples, the Cimbri and Teutones, destroyed a Roman army at Noreia (113) and a series of others in Gaul, culminating at [[battle_of_arausio|Arausio]] on 6 October 105, where the quarrel of the proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio with the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus led to a disaster that Livy's epitomator put at 80,000 soldiers dead.

[[gaius_marius|Gaius Marius]], a new man from Arpinum and Metellus' legate in Africa, rode this crisis. Elected consul for 107 against the Senate's wishes, he was given the African command by popular vote and enrolled volunteers from the propertyless (capite censi). Jugurtha was captured in 105 through the diplomacy of Marius' quaestor, Lucius Cornelius Sulla ([[sulla|Sulla]]). Marius then held five consecutive consulships (104-100), retrained the army, and annihilated the Teutones at [[battle_of_aquae_sextiae|Aquae Sextiae]] (102) and the Cimbri at [[battle_of_vercellae|Vercellae]] (101). The 'Marian reforms' are a modern bundle: recruitment of volunteers continued an older trend of lowering the property qualification, and the cohort as tactical unit probably evolved over decades. What was new was the dependence of poor veterans on their general to obtain land after discharge. In 100 Marius' allies, the tribune Lucius Appuleius Saturninus and the praetor Gaius Servilius Glaucia, used violence to pass veteran colonies; when they murdered a rival candidate, Marius himself suppressed them under another senatus consultum ultimum.

The allied question came to a head in 91. The tribune Marcus Livius Drusus, son of Gaius Gracchus' opponent, proposed a package of jury reform, colonies and citizenship for the Italians; his laws were annulled and he was stabbed in his own house. The allies revolted. In the [[social_war|Social War]] (91-88) the Marsi, Samnites and other peoples formed a state called Italia with its capital at Corfinium and coinage showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf. Velleius put the dead at 300,000. Rome won by fighting and conceding at once: the lex Iulia (90) gave citizenship to communities that stayed loyal or laid down arms, the lex Plautia Papiria (89) to individuals who registered, and the lex Pompeia gave Latin rights to Transpadane Gaul. Italy south of the Po became a single citizen body, though the Senate long delayed distributing the new citizens across all thirty-five tribes.

Meanwhile [[mithridates_vi|Mithridates VI]] of Pontus overran the province of Asia in 89-88 and ordered the massacre of Romans and Italians in a single day, the 'Asiatic Vespers', with victims reckoned at 80,000. When the tribune Publius Sulpicius transferred the command from the consul Sulla to Marius in 88, Sulla marched his six legions on Rome, the first Roman army to take the city. All his officers but one quaestor refused to follow him; the soldiers did. Sulpicius was killed and Marius fled. When Sulla left for the East, the consul Lucius Cornelius Cinna allied with Marius and took Rome by force in 87, killing their enemies; Marius died early in his seventh consulship in January 86.

Sulla, declared a public enemy, nonetheless fought the [[first_mithridatic_war|First Mithridatic War]] in Rome's name. He sacked Athens (1 March 86), won at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, and made the Peace of Dardanus (85), fining Asia 20,000 talents. He returned in 83, joined by the young Gnaeus Pompeius ([[pompey|Pompey]]) with three private legions, and won the civil war at the battle of the Colline Gate (1 November 82). Appointed dictator to write laws and restore the state, he posted lists of the proscribed, whose killers were rewarded and whose property was auctioned; Appian counts 40 senators and 1,600 equites in the first lists, and the final toll ran to thousands. The confiscations, together with veteran settlements of perhaps 80,000 to 120,000 men, rewrote the map of Italian landholding.

Sulla's constitution aimed to make the Senate unassailable. He enlarged it to about 600 by adding equestrians, gave it back the jury courts, created a system of standing criminal courts, raised the quaestors to twenty (who entered the Senate automatically) and praetors to eight, fixed the order and minimum ages of offices, banned re-election to the consulship within ten years, and reduced the tribunate to impotence by barring tribunes from higher office and restricting their legislation. Then, astonishingly, he resigned the dictatorship, held a consulship in 80, and retired to Puteoli, where he died in 78 while writing his memoirs. His epitaph, it was said, claimed that no friend had ever outdone him in kindness or enemy in harm. His settlement would last barely a decade, because the examples he had set, marching on Rome and killing citizens by list, outlived the laws he wrote.
chapters.historiography: The ancient diagnosis was moral decline after the fall of Carthage (Sallust's metus hostilis thesis). Modern work divides between structural explanations (Brunt's agrarian and military crisis, the 'army client' thesis now heavily qualified, Hopkins's demography) and political-cultural ones (Meier's 'crisis without alternative', in which no group could conceive of a different order; Flower's sequence of distinct 'republics'). Mouritsen's Italian Unification overturned the assumption that the allies primarily wanted citizenship, suggesting some aimed at independence; Bispham reconstructs the integration of Italy after the war. The Gracchi have been read as idealists, as factional politicians (Badian), and as heralds of class war; Stockton's account remains a balanced standard. On Sulla, Keaveney's sympathetic biography contrasts with views of the dictatorship as a counter-revolution whose methods destroyed the norms it claimed to restore.

Brunt, The Fall of the Roman Republic and Related Essays (1988)

chapters.title: The Fall of the Republic
chapters.body:
The generation after Sulla is the best-documented period of antiquity. Cicero's speeches, treatises and some 900 letters let us follow politics week by week, and Caesar's own commentaries, Sallust, and later narratives by Plutarch, Appian and Cassius Dio fill the gaps. The paradox of this abundance is that it makes the fall of the Republic seem both overdetermined and contingent. Rome in the 70s had a Senate restored to power, a plebs deprived of tribunes, a vast empire, and a set of military crises that the system could only answer by giving exceptional powers to exceptional men.

The first of these men was [[pompey|Gnaeus Pompeius]], who had raised a private army at twenty-three. The Senate sent him with proconsular imperium, though he had held no office, against [[sertorius|Quintus Sertorius]], the Marian general who led a Romano-Iberian state in Spain from 80 until his murder in 73 or 72. Meanwhile [[spartacus|Spartacus]], a Thracian gladiator, broke out of a school at Capua in 73 with about seventy companions and built an army said to number 70,000 or more, which defeated several Roman armies and ranged from the Alps to Bruttium. [[crassus|Marcus Licinius Crassus]], the richest man in Rome, crushed it in 71 and crucified 6,000 captives along the Via Appia between Capua and Rome. Pompey, returning from Spain, claimed the glory of mopping up. The two rivals combined to win the consulship of 70, in which they restored the tribunes' powers and reformed the juries. Sulla's system had lasted eight years.

In 67 the lex Gabinia gave Pompey a command against the pirates who infested the Mediterranean, with imperium over the whole sea and fifty miles inland, up to 500 ships and some two dozen legates of senatorial rank. He cleared the sea in three months, settling many pirates as farmers. In 66 the lex Manilia, supported by Cicero, transferred to him the war against Mithridates, which Lucius Lucullus had nearly won before his army mutinied. Pompey defeated Mithridates, who fled to the Crimea and killed himself in 63, received the surrender of Tigranes of Armenia, annexed Syria, ending the Seleucid dynasty, entered Jerusalem and the Holy of Holies, and reorganised the East into provinces (Bithynia-Pontus, Cilicia, Syria, Crete) and a ring of client kingdoms. Plutarch reports that he raised the annual revenues of the state from 50 to 85 million denarii.

At home the consul of 63, the new man [[cicero|Marcus Tullius Cicero]], suppressed the conspiracy of Lucius Sergius Catilina, a bankrupt patrician who had twice failed to win the consulship and turned to the indebted and dispossessed, including Sullan veterans. Five conspirators arrested in Rome were executed on 5 December without trial, on the Senate's advice, after [[cato_the_younger|Marcus Porcius Cato]] outargued [[julius_caesar|Julius Caesar]], who had proposed life imprisonment. Catiline died fighting at Pistoria. Cicero's boast that he had saved the state became a liability when his enemy Publius Clodius Pulcher, as tribune in 58, passed a law exiling anyone who had executed citizens without trial.

Pompey returned in 62 and disbanded his army, expecting the Senate to ratify his eastern settlement and give land to his veterans. Led by Cato and Lucullus, it refused. Crassus, representing the publicani who wanted a rebate on the Asian tax contract, was also rebuffed. Caesar, back from Spain, brokered an informal alliance of the three (the 'first triumvirate' is a modern term) and won the consulship of 59. He passed land laws and the eastern acta through the assembly, ignoring the religious obstruction of his colleague Bibulus, who stayed at home 'watching the skies'; wits spoke of the consulship of Julius and Caesar. A law of the tribune Vatinius gave him Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years; the Senate added Transalpine Gaul.

Caesar's [[gallic_wars|Gallic Wars]] (58-50) were a war of conquest presented as defence. Over eight seasons he defeated the Helvetii and the German Ariovistus, conquered the Belgae and the Veneti, bridged the Rhine twice and crossed twice to Britain, and finally broke the great revolt of [[vercingetorix|Vercingetorix]] at the [[siege_of_alesia|siege of Alesia]] (52), where his double line of fortifications held off a relieving army. Plutarch gives a million killed and a million enslaved; the figures are rhetorical but the scale of destruction was real. The Commentaries, sent back year by year, made Caesar's victories a political campaign at Rome.

The city meanwhile became ungovernable. Clodius organised the urban plebs through the restored neighbourhood associations (collegia), made the grain ration free, and fought street battles with the gangs of Titus Annius Milo. Elections were repeatedly postponed by violence and bribery. The coalition was renewed at Luca in 56; Pompey and Crassus held a second consulship in 55 and took five-year commands in Spain and Syria. In 54 Pompey's wife Julia, Caesar's daughter, died; in 53 Crassus and his army were destroyed by the Parthians at [[battle_of_carrhae|Carrhae]]. In January 52 Clodius was killed by Milo's men on the Via Appia, and his followers burned the Senate house as his funeral pyre. The Senate made Pompey sole consul.

The final crisis turned on the timing of Caesar's return. He wanted to pass directly from his command to a second consulship, retaining immunity from prosecution; his enemies, led by Cato, meant to try him as a private citizen. In December 50 the Senate voted 370 to 22 that both Caesar and Pompey should lay down their commands, but the consuls ignored it. On 7 January 49 the Senate passed the last decree; on 10 or 11 January Caesar crossed the Rubicon with one legion. Pompey and most of the Senate abandoned Italy. Caesar defeated the Pompeian army in Spain at Ilerda, crossed to Greece, survived a defeat at Dyrrhachium, and destroyed Pompey's larger army at [[battle_of_pharsalus|Pharsalus]] on 9 August 48. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on landing. Caesar, following him, became entangled in the Alexandrian War and the cause of [[cleopatra_vii|Cleopatra VII]], then crushed Pharnaces at Zela ('veni, vidi, vici'), the Pompeians in Africa at Thapsus (46), where Cato killed himself at Utica, and in Spain at Munda (45).

As dictator Caesar governed energetically. He reformed the calendar (the Julian year of 365 days from 1 January 45), enlarged the Senate to 900, raised the number of praetors to sixteen and quaestors to forty, cut the grain dole from 320,000 to 150,000 recipients, founded colonies for veterans and poor citizens at Carthage, Corinth and elsewhere, enfranchised Gades and the Transpadanes, and planned a new forum, a library and a campaign against Parthia. His clemency towards defeated enemies was itself an assertion of monarchical power. In February 44 he became dictator for life. On the Ides of March he was stabbed twenty-three times in the Senate meeting in the Curia of Pompey by some sixty conspirators led by [[brutus_assassin|Marcus Brutus]] and [[cassius|Gaius Cassius]].

The assassins had no plan beyond liberty. [[mark_antony|Mark Antony]], the surviving consul, outmanoeuvred them, but Caesar's will made his great-nephew Gaius Octavius, aged eighteen, his adopted son and heir. Octavian ([[augustus|Augustus]]) raised an army from Caesar's veterans, allied with the Senate and Cicero against Antony in the War of Mutina (43), then marched on Rome to take the consulship and joined Antony and [[lepidus_triumvir|Lepidus]] in the triumvirate legalised by the lex Titia (27 November 43). Their proscriptions claimed about 300 senators and 2,000 equites, among them Cicero, whose head and hands were nailed to the Rostra. At [[battle_of_philippi|Philippi]] (October 42) Brutus and Cassius were defeated and killed.

The triumvirs divided the world. Octavian took on the thankless task of settling veterans in Italy, which led to the Perusine War against Antony's brother (41-40); the pact of Brundisium (40) gave Antony the East and Octavian the West, sealed by Antony's marriage to Octavia. [[agrippa|Agrippa]] defeated [[sextus_pompey|Sextus Pompey]], who had held Sicily and starved Rome, at Naulochus in 36, and Lepidus was pushed aside. Antony's Parthian invasion of 36 ended in a costly retreat, and his alliance with Cleopatra, the Donations of Alexandria (34) granting territories to her children, and his will (read out by Octavian) allowed Octavian to frame the coming war as Rome against an Egyptian queen. All Italy swore an oath of loyalty to Octavian. At [[battle_of_actium|Actium]] on 2 September 31 Agrippa's fleet broke Antony's; Cleopatra and Antony escaped to Egypt and killed themselves in August 30 when Octavian took Alexandria. Egypt became Roman. After a century of crisis, one man controlled all the armies of the empire.
chapters.historiography: Syme's The Roman Revolution (1939) told the fall as the triumph of a faction led by a ruthless dynast and his partisans, in prose modelled on Tacitus. Gruen's The Last Generation of the Roman Republic (1974) argued that the Republic's institutions were functioning until the civil war of 49, which itself was not inevitable: the Republic fell because of the war, not the war because of the Republic's fall. Brunt and Hopkins stressed structural causes (land, the army, the urban plebs); Meier's 'crisis without alternative' explains why no reform could be conceived within the political culture. Morstein-Marx and Millar have revived the importance of the people and public oratory; Tatum and Lintott studied violence and Clodius' organisation. Caesar's aims (monarchy on the Hellenistic model or a pragmatic dictatorship) and the role of Cleopatra remain debated.

chapters.title: Augustus and the Making of the Principate
chapters.body:
Augustus ruled for forty-four years, longer than any Roman before or after him, and created a system that lasted for three centuries with modifications. His own account of it, the Res Gestae Divi Augusti, inscribed on bronze pillars before his mausoleum and copied in the provinces (the best text survives on the walls of the temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra), claims that he transferred the state from his own power to the judgement of the Senate and people, and thereafter excelled all in authority (auctoritas) but had no more power (potestas) than his colleagues in each magistracy. The truth was subtler and harder. He held, in a combination never seen before, powers that each had republican precedent; and he held the army.

The constitutional settlement came in stages. In January 27 BC Octavian 'restored the res publica' and received in return a ten-year command over a large provincia comprising Spain, Gaul, Syria and Egypt, where most of the legions were stationed, and on 16 January the name Augustus, 'revered', with its religious associations. He held the consulship every year until 23 BC, when, after a near-fatal illness and a conspiracy (the date and identity of Varro Murena are debated), he resigned it and took instead the tribunician power (tribunicia potestas), by which he dated his reign, and an imperium superior to that of other proconsuls (maius). He became pontifex maximus in 12 BC after Lepidus died, and pater patriae in 2 BC. The model was not a written constitution but an accumulation of grants, renewed at intervals, which made his position look like a magistracy while it functioned as a monarchy.

The army was reformed into a standing professional force. Of some sixty legions under arms after Actium, Augustus kept twenty-eight (twenty-five after AD 9), about 150,000 citizen soldiers, with a roughly equal number of non-citizen auxiliaries in cohorts and cavalry alae, and fleets at Misenum and Ravenna. Terms of service were fixed (sixteen years, later twenty plus reserve service), and in AD 6 a military treasury (aerarium militare) was founded with 170 million sesterces from his own funds and financed thereafter by a 5 per cent inheritance tax and a 1 per cent sales tax, so that veterans received cash bounties rather than confiscated land. In Rome nine praetorian cohorts guarded the emperor, three urban cohorts policed the city, and in AD 6 seven cohorts of vigiles took over firefighting. The legions moved to the frontiers, out of politics for a century.

Administration of the empire was divided. 'Public' provinces, mostly peaceful and without legions (Africa, Asia, Achaea, Baetica and others), were governed by senatorial proconsuls chosen by lot; 'imperial' provinces were governed by Augustus' own legates. Egypt, the granary and too dangerous to entrust to a senator, was ruled by an equestrian prefect; senators needed permission even to visit it. The equestrian order found a new career in the emperor's service as prefects and procurators managing his property and revenues, and freedmen of the imperial household ran its accounts. Censuses of the provinces (the one in Judaea in AD 6 under Quirinius is famous from Luke's gospel) laid the basis for regular direct taxation. Tribute exactions became more predictable; extortion trials continued.

Augustus remade the senatorial order. He purged the Senate in 28 and 18 BC, reducing it from over 1,000 to about 600, fixed a property qualification of a million sesterces, and gave it new functions as a court and a source of decrees with the force of law. Senators still governed provinces, commanded legions as legates, and held consulships, now shared with suffect consuls each year so that more men could reach consular rank. Political careers were safe, prestigious and dependent on imperial favour. Elections continued, under supervision, until Tiberius transferred them to the Senate in AD 14.

Social legislation sought to restore the moral and demographic health of the citizen elite. The Julian laws of 18 BC and the lex Papia Poppaea of AD 9 penalised celibacy and childlessness in inheritance and rewarded parents of three children (ius trium liberorum); adultery became a public crime with a standing court. Augustus' own daughter Julia was exiled for adultery in 2 BC, and her daughter in AD 8. The poet Ovid, author of the Art of Love, was relegated to Tomis on the Black Sea the same year 'for a poem and a mistake'. The laws were widely evaded; their importance lies in the claim that the private life of citizens was the ruler's business.

Religion and image-making were central. Augustus claimed to have restored eighty-two temples in a single year (28 BC). The Ludi Saeculares of 17 BC, with Horace's Carmen Saeculare sung by twenty-seven boys and twenty-seven girls, proclaimed a new age. In 7 BC Rome was reorganised into fourteen regions and 265 neighbourhoods (vici) whose magistrates, often freedmen, worshipped the Lares Augusti and the emperor's Genius. In the provinces the cult of Rome and Augustus spread from Pergamum and Nicomedia (29 BC) to the altar at Lugdunum for the Three Gauls (12 or 10 BC). Paul Zanker showed how a new visual language, on coins, the Ara Pacis Augustae (dedicated 9 BC), the Forum of Augustus with its temple of Mars Ultor and galleries of Roman heroes (2 BC), and household objects, communicated peace, piety and the Julian descent from Venus. Suetonius records the boast that he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble; Agrippa's aqueducts, baths and Pantheon did as much as Augustus' own building. Virgil's Aeneid, Horace's Odes, Livy's history and Propertius' elegies created a literature that was not merely propaganda but debated what Rome had become.

Expansion continued at a pace that rivalled Caesar's. Northern Spain was finally subdued in 19 BC; the Alps and Raetia were conquered by Tiberius and Drusus in 15 BC; the Danube frontier was secured in Illyricum and Pannonia; Galatia was annexed in 25 BC; and Drusus campaigned to the Elbe (12-9 BC). A province of Germania seemed close to organisation when the great Pannonian revolt of AD 6-9 tied down half the army, and in September AD 9 Publius Quinctilius Varus and three legions were destroyed by [[arminius|Arminius]] in the [[battle_of_teutoburg_forest|Teutoburg Forest]]. Excavations at Kalkriese near Osnabrück since 1987 have located at least part of the battlefield. Augustus is said to have cried 'Varus, give me back my legions'; his last advice to his successor was to keep the empire within its existing bounds.

The weakness of the system was succession, which had no legal basis. Augustus groomed in turn his nephew Marcellus (died 23 BC), his friend Agrippa (died 12 BC), and Agrippa's sons by Julia, Gaius and Lucius Caesar, whom he adopted; both died young (AD 2 and 4). He turned at last to his stepson [[tiberius|Tiberius]], son of [[livia|Livia]], adopted in AD 4 and given tribunician power and equal imperium. When Augustus died at Nola on 19 August AD 14, aged seventy-five, the transfer of power was smooth. The Senate deified him. The Principate had survived its founder, and with it the illusion that the Republic still existed.
chapters.historiography: Syme's Augustus was a revolutionary leader of a faction who disguised autocracy as restoration; Millar's work on the emperor's practical role and Eck's concise biography presented a ruler responding to petitions and circumstances. Wallace-Hadrill and Galinsky stressed Augustan cultural transformation as a negotiated redefinition of Roman identity, while Zanker's visual analysis opened a new field. Constitutional debates concern the 'settlements' of 27 and 23, the nature of imperium maius, and whether Augustus intended a dynasty from the start. The Teutoburg disaster and the 'Augustan grand strategy' (Luttwak; contested by Whittaker and Isaac) raise the question whether Augustus meant to stop expanding or was merely forced to. Recent scholarship (Osgood) has also emphasised the long triumviral period as the real crucible of the regime.

Zanker, The Power of Images in the Age of Augustus (1988)
